---
title: "Perimeter Runs and Misdirection: Jet Sweeps, Reverses, and the Wing-T's Children"
subtitle: "How offenses win the race to the sideline, and how they punish a defense that runs too hard to win it back"
description: "The outside run game and its mirror image: why the edge is a race, the two perimeter blocks (crack and seal) and the crack-toss, the jet sweep and what it does to linebackers, the end-around and the reverse, the Delaware Wing-T's buck sweep, series football and the waggle, 'eye candy' that freezes a linebacker for half a second, how defenses answer, what the numbers say about receivers carrying the ball, and why all of it is a constraint on everything else an offense does."
glossary:
  "Jet sweep": "A run in which a receiver (or back) in jet motion takes a handoff, or a tiny forward flip, from the quarterback at full speed as he crosses the formation, and races for the edge on the side he is running toward."
  "End-around": "A run in which a receiver who lined up outside comes back behind the line and takes a handoff from the quarterback, carrying the ball toward the other side of the field. One exchange; often paired with a fake run the opposite way."
  "Reverse": "A run in which the ball is first given to a player running one way and then handed or pitched to a teammate running the other way, so the ball changes direction behind the line. Two exchanges; a double reverse adds a third."
  "Crack-toss": "A toss sweep on which a receiver lined up outside the play blocks back inside (a crack block) on the defender responsible for the edge, while a pulling lineman replaces him on the cornerback."
  "Crack-and-replace": "The pairing of blocks on a perimeter run in which a receiver leaves the defender he would normally block (usually the cornerback) to crack inside, and a pulling lineman replaces him on that defender."
  "Crack block": "A block by a player lined up outside the play, usually a wide receiver or wingback, who comes back toward the ball and hits a defender (often a linebacker or safety watching the ball) from the side. In the NFL it must be above the waist and not to the head or neck."
  "Seal block": "A block whose job is to wall a defender off from the ball carrier's path rather than to move him: usually pinning an inside defender inside so the run can go outside him."
  "Buck sweep": "The signature play of the Wing-T: the halfback sweeps toward the wingback's side behind both guards, who pull (one kicks out the end man, the other turns up inside him), while the tight end and wingback block down and the fullback fakes a plunge ('buck') up the middle."
  "Series football": "Building an offense from groups of plays that begin with the same backfield action and end differently, each one designed to beat the defense's reaction to another, so the defense cannot tell which play it is from the first second."
  Misdirection: "Any play design that gets the defense to commit in one direction, with motion, fakes or the flow of the line, while the ball goes another way."
  "Eye candy": "Motion and fakes by players who will not get the ball, designed to pull defenders' eyes and first steps the wrong way so the real play gains a fraction of a second or a gap."
  Waggle: "The Wing-T's play-action bootleg: the quarterback fakes a run one way (classically the buck sweep) and rolls out the other way behind both guards, who pull to that side to protect him, with receivers at short, medium and deep levels on that side, so he can run or throw. The ancestor of the NFL bootleg."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"
#| output: false
import os
import shutil
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, RegularPolygon
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, technique, style

style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
GREEN = "#0f7a55"          # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]   # a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange
LINE_D, OFF_D = -0.7, -1.5  # "on the line" and "a yard off it" (only the ends of the line may be receivers)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ building plays by hand
def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label if label is not None else key)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line():
    """The five offensive linemen, labelled so the reader can follow the pullers."""
    return [O(k, k, LINE_D, w) for k, w in (("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2))]


def check_legal(players):
    """Seven on the line, and only the two end men of the line may be receivers."""
    off = [p for p in players if p.side == "off"]
    on = sorted([p for p in off if p.d > -1.0], key=lambda p: p.w)
    assert len(off) == 11 and len(on) == 7, f"{len(off)} players, {len(on)} on the line"
    for p in on[1:-1]:
        assert p.pos in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"), f"{p.key} is covered up but is a receiver"
    return players


def front(pe=("9", 5.7), pt=("3", 2.35), bt=("1", -0.7), be=("5", -4.0), lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"),
          ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M")), extra=(), cb=(-12.0, 12.0), safeties=((12.0, -8.0), (12.0, 8.0))):
    """A generic four-man front, linemen labelled by technique number (03-01), plus linebackers and DBs.
    Fronts get their names in Part 5; here they are just people to block."""
    out = [D("DE_L", "DE", 1.0, be[1], be[0]), D("DT_L", "DT", 1.0, bt[1], bt[0]),
           D("DT_R", "DT", 1.0, pt[1], pt[0]), D("DE_R", "DE", 1.0, pe[1], pe[0])]
    out += [D(k, k, d, w, lab) for k, d, w, lab in lbs]
    out += [D(k, pos, d, w, lab) for k, pos, d, w, lab in extra]
    out += [D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, cb[0], "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, cb[1], "CB"),
            D("FS", "FS", *safeties[0], "FS"), D("SS", "SS", *safeties[1], "SS")]
    return out


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, pull, path or run."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "pull":
        return p.pull(key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "route":
        return p.route(key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed, frame="field")
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def motion_to(p, key, via, end, speed=6.0):
    """Pre-snap motion through absolute points, ending where the player is when the ball is snapped."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    return p.motion(key, pts=[tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)], speed=speed)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ drawing helpers
def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def clean(ax):
    """Box-zoomed diagrams: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip text to the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=6.2, ax=None, **kw):
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    return fld


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.2, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=12, fontweight=weight,
                linespacing=1.15, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=12, linespacing=1.15,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=6),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))


def flow(fld, p, pts, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, alpha=0.9, ls=(0, (2.5, 1.8))):
    """A defender's reaction, drawn as a dashed orange arrow through absolute (d, w) points."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=5, alpha=alpha)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                                     color=color, lw=lw, zorder=5, alpha=alpha))


def dashed(fld, p, pts, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.4):
    """Hand-drawn pre-snap motion: dashed blue with a solid head."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=5)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9,
                                     color=color, lw=lw, zorder=5))


def ghost(fld, p, d, w, label, side="def"):
    """A hollow dashed marker: where a player was, or would have been."""
    x, y = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, d, w))
    col = style.DEFENSE if side == "def" else style.OFFENSE
    if side == "def":
        pat = RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=0.94, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.1,
                             ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), zorder=6)
    else:
        pat = Circle((x, y), 0.75, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), zorder=6)
    fld.ax.add_patch(pat)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", color=col, fontweight="bold", zorder=6, fontsize=6.3)


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ frame strips (PDF) and video (web)
MARK_R = 0.78   # frame-strip marker radius in yards


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=(), ghosts=None, decorate=None):
    """One moment of a simulated play: markers, faint trails, rings, and optional hollow 'ghosts'
    (players from a second version of the play, at the same moment)."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 1.0, play.los + window[1] - 1.0)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 1.0, yhi - 1.0)]
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(set(shown["_id"])) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    if ghosts is not None and t > 0.05:
        gplay, gkeys = ghosts
        for k in gkeys:
            x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*gplay.position(k, t))))
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc="none",
                                        ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), zorder=6))
            glab = str(gplay.players[k].label)
            ax.text(x, y, glab, ha="center", va="center", color=style.DEFENSE, fontweight="bold", zorder=6,
                    fontsize=max(4.5, min(8.0, ppy * (0.95 if len(glab) <= 1 else 0.75))))
    if decorate is not None:
        decorate(ax, fld, t)
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        if r["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.45), 0.7, 0.42, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=11))
            continue
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.5, min(8.5, ppy * (0.95 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.75)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        rr = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(rr["x"], rr["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.3, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    return fld


def strip(play, times, notes, lateral, window, ncols=2, rings=(), ghosts=None, width_in=6.5, decorate=None):
    """The print version of an animation: numbered panels with a caption under each."""
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False, figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + 0.6)))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, ghosts, decorate)
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"), fontsize=8.5,
                     color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.5,
                color=style.INK, linespacing=1.15)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2.4, w_pad=0.8)
    return fig


def video(play, times, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), ghosts=None, width_in=5.6, decorate=None):
    """Web version of the strip: the same panel at every frame, the strip's notes as running captions."""
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, ghosts, decorate)
        cur = [n for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
        txt = ("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s") + (("   " + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else "")
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=8, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=sorted(df["frameId"].unique()), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animated(play, times, notes, **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if PDF:
        strip(play, times, notes, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        video(play, times, notes, **kw)
```

Third quarter, second-and-8. For the fourth time today a receiver sprints across the formation in
jet motion just as the ball is snapped. The first time he got the ball and ran around the left end
for eleven yards. The next two times the quarterback stuck the ball in his belly and pulled it out,
and both linebackers took three hard steps toward him anyway, while the running back went the other
way. This time both linebackers sprint left again, the safety on that side races up to meet the
receiver at the corner, and the quarterback hands the ball to the running back going right, into a
hole where a linebacker stood a moment ago. Nobody on the left side of the field touched the ball,
and every one of them helped make the play. This chapter is about why the defense keeps chasing a
receiver who mostly doesn't get the ball, and what happens to defenses that stop.

**You'll be able to:**

- Explain why runs to the edge are a race, and name the defender each one is trying to outrun or
  wall off.
- Recognize the jet sweep, the end-around, the reverse, the crack-toss and the buck sweep, and say
  what each one punishes.
- Spot the two perimeter blocks (the **crack** and the **seal**) and say why a receiver blocking back
  toward the ball is one of the most effective blocks in football.
- Explain the Wing-T's series logic (buck sweep, trap, waggle, counter) and point to its NFL
  descendants on a Sunday broadcast.
- Watch the linebackers on jet motion and say whether the motion did its job, even when the ball went
  somewhere else.
- Explain why a play that gains a lot when it's run rarely can't simply be run more often.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[Gap Schemes](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)**: a [**pull**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pull)
  is a lineman leaving his spot at the snap to block somewhere else; a
  [puller](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) either **kicks out** the end man (hits him from the inside and
  pushes him toward the sideline) or **logs** him (gets outside him and pins him in). The
  [toss](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) is a pitch to a back already running wide, and
  [pin-and-pull](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) is the modern outside run in which the linemen nearest
  the play block down (pin) and the ones farther away pull around them.
  [Trap](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) lets a defender in and hits him from the side with a pulling
  lineman; [counter](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) starts the backfield one way and pulls blockers back
  the other.
- **[Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)**:
  [**jet motion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jet-motion) is a receiver sprinting flat across the
  formation with the snap timed just before he reaches the quarterback, and
  [fly motion](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fly-motion) is the Wing-T coaches' name for the same thing
  (the fly sweep was born outside the Wing-T and adopted by it; more below).
  Against motion the defense can *travel* (one defender follows), *bump* (everyone slides a spot) or
  *spin* (a safety comes down toward the motion and the other goes to the middle).
- From earlier chapters: [play side and backside](03-01-run-game-language.qmd) (the half of the
  formation the run is aimed at, and the other half), the [technique numbers](03-01-run-game-language.qmd)
  used to label defensive linemen (a 1 or 3 is on a guard's shoulder, a 5 outside a tackle, a 7 on the
  tight end's inside shoulder, a 9 outside him), the
  [Wing-T formation](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd) (a wingback just outside
  and behind the tight end), and the [condensed formation](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)
  (receivers lined up close to the line, where they can block back inside).
:::

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares; *left* and *right* are
always the offense's. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the five offensive linemen, Q the quarterback, R the
running back, Y the tight end, and X, Z and H receivers (each caption says where they line up). In the
Wing-T pictures F is the fullback, H the halfback and WB the wingback. Defensive linemen are labelled by
technique number; W and M are the Will and Mike linebackers, S the Sam, NB the nickel back, CB a
cornerback, FS and SS the safeties. Lines ending in a short bar are blocks, arrows are paths, the thick
dark arrow is the ball carrier, and dashed orange arrows are how the defense reacts.

## The edge is a race

Everything you have seen in the run game so far has been a fight in a phone booth. On
[inside zone](03-02-zone-running.qmd) or [power](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd), blockers and defenders
start a yard apart, and the run hits before the defense can move very far. Runs to the **perimeter**,
the edge of the formation and the open grass outside it, are a different contest. The ball carrier
has 10 or 15 yards of sideways running to do before he can turn upfield, and every defender on the
field has time to see where he is going and run there too. An outside run is a race between the
ball and the defense's **pursuit**, the whole team running to the ball.

The defense organizes that race with two jobs. One defender on each side is the **force** player
(more on him in [Run Fits](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)): his
job is to get outside the ball and turn it back inside, toward everyone else. Everyone else pursues,
each on an [angle](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd) aimed
at where the ball carrier *will be*, not where he is. If the force player holds and the pursuit is
fast, an outside run dies for no gain or a loss, and losing yards behind the line is the outside run's
signature failure.

Who is the force player? The coverage decides, so it changes from snap to snap, but a rule of thumb
gets you most of the way: **he is usually the outermost defender standing near the line on that side.**
That is often an outside linebacker or a nickel back lined up outside the tight end or slot. If a safety
has walked down to about seven or eight yards deep outside the formation, it's probably him. If the
cornerback is squatting at five yards with a safety deep behind him (the look of
[Cover 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd)), the corner is the force. You'll hear a
close cousin, [*contain*](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd).
Both mean "nothing gets outside me." Coaches say *force* for the defender who meets a run coming at him
and turns it in, and *contain* for the man whose rule is to keep the ball, or a scrambling quarterback,
from ever getting outside him. That matters most on the side the play is leaving, as you'll see.

So the defense wants to pursue *fast*. And that is the opening for everything else in this chapter.
A defense that flows hard to stop the sweep leaves the other side of the field empty and its
linebackers a step out of place. The offense can punish that in two ways: run the ball back where the
defense came from, or simply make the defense *think* the ball is going somewhere it isn't.

```{python}
#| label: fig-edge-dilemma
#| fig-cap: "The defense's dilemma on an outside run to the right (here a toss from under center; the two receivers, X and Z, are split wide). Left: if the defenders read and react slowly, the back gets outside the end before the linebackers and the safety arrive, and the race is lost. Right: if they all sprint to the ball at the snap (dashed orange arrows), the Sam and the safety beat the back to the edge and he is tackled behind the line (red X). But the left side of the field is now empty (green shading) and the linebackers have run themselves out of the middle. Plays that go back that way, or fake one way and go the other, exist to punish the fast defense."
def dilemma(ax, fast):
    off = check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.5, 0.0, "R"),
                                O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.8),
                                O("X", "WR", OFF_D, -12.0), O("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 12.0)])
    dfn = front(pe=("9", 5.7), be=("9", -5.7), lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.4, "M"),
                                                    ("SAM", 4.5, 4.9, "S")),
                safeties=((12.0, -6.0), (8.0, 8.0)), cb=(-12.0, 12.0))
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.pitch("RB", t=0.3)
    if fast:   # caught at the edge, a yard and a half behind the line
        go_to(p, "RB", (-1.6, 8.4), "run", via=[(-5.6, 3.5), (-3.6, 7.0)])
    else:
        go_to(p, "RB", (8.0, 10.0), "run", via=[(-5.6, 3.5), (-3.8, 7.5), (-0.5, 9.5)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-2.6, 0.9), "path")
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y", "U"):
        q = p.players[k]
        go_to(p, k, (0.1, q.w + 1.1))
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-14.5, 14.5), window=(-8.8, 12.5), title=False)
    if fast:
        for pts in ([(4.5, -2.4), (3.6, 1.0), (2.6, 5.6)], [(4.5, 1.4), (3.4, 5.3), (2.2, 7.6)],
                    [(4.5, 4.9), (0.0, 8.3)], [(8.0, 8.0), (1.4, 9.4)], [(12.0, -6.0), (10.5, 2.0), (7.5, 7.0)],
                    [(1.0, -5.7), (-1.8, -5.2), (-3.8, -1.4)]):
            flow(fld, p, pts)
        xm, ym = _P(fld, p, -1.0, 9.3)
        fld.ax.text(float(xm), float(ym), "\u2715", color=style.SERIES[7],
                    fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center", zorder=13)
        x0, y0 = _P(fld, p, 3.0, -6.0)
        fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x0), float(y0)), 8.0, 12.0, fc=GREEN, alpha=0.13, ec=GREEN, lw=1.0,
                                 ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.5))
        say(fld, p, 9.6, -5.6, "left side:\nnobody home", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.2, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -5.6, -8.4, "the end chases\nfrom behind", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -6.4, 9.6, "caught behind\nthe line", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
    else:
        for pts in ([(4.5, -2.4), (4.3, -0.6)], [(4.5, 1.4), (4.2, 3.2)], [(4.5, 4.9), (4.0, 6.6)],
                    [(8.0, 8.0), (7.2, 9.0)], [(12.0, -6.0), (11.7, -4.2)]):
            flow(fld, p, pts)
        say(fld, p, 9.6, 3.0, "linebackers wait\nto be sure", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        say(fld, p, -6.6, 9.4, "the back\nwins the edge", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
    ax.set_title("Defense reacts slowly" if not fast else "Defense flies to the ball", fontsize=9, loc="left",
                 color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
dilemma(axes[0], False)
dilemma(axes[1], True)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

**Perimeter runs** punish a defense that is slow to the edge. **[Misdirection](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-misdirection)**, any play design that gets
the defense to commit in one direction while the ball goes another, punishes a defense that is fast
to it. The two families need each other: misdirection only works if the defense has a reason to run
hard, and the only reason it has is that the perimeter run will beat it if it doesn't.

## The perimeter blocks: crack and seal

Outside runs need two kinds of block that you haven't met yet, because inside runs rarely need them.

A [**crack block**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-crack-block) is a block thrown by a player lined
up *outside* the play, usually a wide receiver or a wingback, who comes back *toward the ball* and hits
a defender from the side. The usual target is a linebacker or safety who is watching the ball carrier
and running to the edge, which is why the block is so effective: the defender's eyes are on the ball,
his momentum is going outside, and the blocker arrives from a direction he isn't looking. You saw one
animated in [02-04](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd), where a
condensed split put the receiver close enough to crack in a step or two.

A [**seal block**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-seal-block) is any block whose job is to *wall a
defender off* from the ball's path, rather than to move him. On an outside run that usually means
pinning an inside defender inside: the tight end steps down onto an end lined up on his inside
shoulder, gets his body between that end and the sideline, and the back runs outside the wall. A seal
doesn't need to drive the defender back a yard; it only needs to stay in the way while the ball goes by.
Coaches use the word loosely (a [log block](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) by a puller who gets outside a
defender and pins him in is a kind of seal), but the idea is always the same: *you don't move him, you
shut him off.*

The two blocks together make the classic outside run of the modern NFL, the
[**crack-toss**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-crack-toss). 02-04's animation showed the crack and the
puller. Here are the parts it skipped: the seal, exactly who replaces whom, and (after the figure) the
rule that governs the crack and the defense's answer to it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-crack-seal
#| fig-cap: "Crack-toss right from a condensed two-tight-end set (12 personnel; Z lines up only about 8½ yards from the ball, a yard off the line). The quarterback tosses to the back (R) heading right. Z (green ring) cracks back inside on the Sam linebacker (S), the force player. The purple rings are the two blockers who make the crack possible: the tight end Y seals the 7-technique end lined up on his inside shoulder, and the right guard pulls behind the line and replaces Z on the cornerback, kicking him out as he comes up. The right tackle blocks down on the 3-technique so the guard can leave (pin-and-pull). The back turns up in the lane between the crack and the kick-out; the safety (SS) is the defender left over. Backside, the linemen and the second tight end (U) cut off pursuit."
off = check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.5, -0.5, "R"),
                            O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.8),
                            O("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 8.6), O("X", "WR", OFF_D, -9.5)])
dfn = front(pe=("7", 4.2), pt=("3", 2.35), bt=("1", -0.7), be=("5", -4.0),
            lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.4, "M"), ("SAM", 4.2, 7.0, "S")),
            cb=(-11.0, 12.6), safeties=((12.0, -6.5), (11.0, 7.0)))
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Crack-toss: the crack, the seal and the replace")
p.pitch("RB", t=0.3)
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.7, 1.0), "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "RB", (12.5, 10.3), "run", via=[(-5.8, 3.0), (-5.2, 6.2), (-4.2, 8.6), (-2.6, 10.1)])
go_to(p, "Z", (3.4, 7.5), via=[(-0.2, 8.2)])                       # the crack, from the side
go_to(p, "Y", (0.2, 4.5), via=[(-0.3, 5.0)])                       # the seal: step down, stay outside him
go_to(p, "RG", (3.8, 12.0), "pull", via=[(-1.9, 2.6), (-2.8, 6.0), (-2.9, 8.6), (-1.4, 11.0)])   # pull and replace
go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.6), via=[(-0.4, 3.0)])                      # pin the 3
go_to(p, "C", (3.2, 1.4), via=[(-0.2, 0.7)])                       # climb to the Mike
go_to(p, "LG", (0.5, -0.1), via=[(-0.4, -0.9)])                    # cut off the 1
go_to(p, "LT", (3.2, -1.8), via=[(-0.4, -2.6)])                    # climb to the Will
go_to(p, "U", (0.4, -3.4), via=[(-0.5, -4.4)])                     # cut off the backside end
go_to(p, "X", (8.0, -10.0), "route")                               # run the corner off
p.highlight("Y", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-14.0, 17.5), window=(-8.5, 14.5))
zx, zy = _P(fld, p, -1.5, 8.6)                                     # a snug ring on Z, clear of the pull path
fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(zx), float(zy)), 0.98, fc="none", ec=GREEN, lw=2.0, zorder=3.5))
flow(fld, p, [(6.5, 12.6), (4.8, 12.5)], lw=1.3)                   # the corner comes up
point_to(fld, p, (8.4, 4.4), (3.6, 7.3), "crack", color=GREEN, fontsize=7.4)
point_to(fld, p, (3.3, 4.5), (0.5, 4.5), "seal", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7.4)
point_to(fld, p, (8.4, 15.6), (3.9, 12.1), "replace\n(kick-out)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7.2)
point_to(fld, p, (-6.4, 13.4), (-2.8, 7.4), "RG's pull", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -6.6, -6.8, "backside: cut off\nthe pursuit", fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-crack-seal as a list of problems and answers. The Sam linebacker lined up outside the tight
end is the defense's force player: if he gets outside the ball, the toss is dead. Nobody on the line
can reach him in time, but Z, lined up just outside him, can hit him from the side before he gets
going. The end is lined up on the tight end's inside shoulder (a 7-technique), so Y only has to keep him
there: one step down, body between the end and the sideline, and hold. (If the end were lined up
*outside* Y, in a 9, keeping him inside would take a *reach*, the hardest block a tight end is asked to
make, and offenses usually build a different answer for that look.) The cornerback is now unblocked, so
a lineman pulls around both blocks to get him. That's
[**crack-and-replace**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-crack-and-replace): the receiver leaves his
usual man to crack inside, and a puller replaces him.

Who pulls varies, and this is why the 02-04 animation pulled the guard. Here the right tackle blocks
down on the 3-technique and the right guard pulls behind him, the [pin-and-pull](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)
logic of 03-03: the tackle has the better angle on the 3, the guard is free to go. Some teams pull the
tackle instead, which is a shorter trip, as long as the guard can handle the 3 on his own; some pull
both, and the second puller goes after the safety who is left over here. Every block on the play is an
angle the defender wasn't expecting.

The cost is that crack-toss is fragile in two specific ways. If the cracked defender sees it coming, he
can duck under the crack and be in the backfield, and the puller has to choose between him and the
corner. And the cornerback has an answer of his own: when he sees the receiver go inside, he yells
"crack!" and comes up hard to take the force job himself. The puller still has him to block, but he now
meets him sooner and tighter than planned, can only kick him out, and the back is forced to cut up
inside, back toward the pursuit, instead of getting around the edge.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"A crack block is a cheap shot." A *legal* crack is a hands-first block, from the side and chest-high,
aimed at the defender's near number or armpit on the side he's facing. Receivers practise it the way
linemen practise down blocks. What's illegal is hitting him low, hitting him in the head or neck, or
leading with the shoulder, and if all the blocker can see is the back of the defender's jersey, it isn't
a crack at all but a block in the back (10 yards), so a well-coached receiver lets that man go and finds
another.[^backblock]

The rules are strict because a defender hit from the side by a player running at him can't protect
himself. The crackback rule (Rule 12, Section 2, Article 6) covers a player who lines up more than two
yards outside the tackle, or starts in the backfield and is in motion or moves out that wide, and then
blocks back toward the spot of the snap: within five yards of the line of scrimmage he may not hit a
defender below the waist, nor in the head or neck (or in any other way banned against a defenseless
player). It costs 15 yards.[^crackrule] Since 2019 a separate rule has also banned any *blindside* block,
a forcible hit with the helmet, forearm or shoulder thrown while the blocker's path is toward or parallel
to his own end line, outside the tight area around the snap,[^blindside] and from the 2026 season
blindside blocks are one of the five fouls in the league's three-strike suspension policy (three in a
season means a one-game suspension).[^threestrike] A crack runs parallel to the line, which is why the
shoulder shot is gone and the hands-first block is the only kind you'll see.
:::

## The jet sweep: a running start at the edge

The [**jet sweep**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jet-sweep) is the purest perimeter play: a
receiver in [jet motion](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jet-motion) takes the ball from the
quarterback without slowing down and races for the edge on the side he's heading toward. You met the
motion and the defense's three answers to it (travel, bump, spin) in
[02-06](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd). This section is about the run itself,
and about what it does to the linebackers.

Three things make it work:

- **The running start.** The receiver is already at full speed when the ball is snapped; the
  defenders start from a standstill. The simple model in 02-06 put the gap at about three yards after
  one second. On a play that is a race to the corner, three yards is the race.
- **The angle.** He takes the ball roughly in front of the quarterback, and within a stride or two he
  is past the far guard, already outside the box and heading for the edge. The defense's force player
  has to cover more ground than he does.
- **What it does to everyone else.** Linebackers are taught to read *keys*: usually a guard, the
  running back, or the backfield as a whole, depending on the defense
  ([05-04](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd) covers which).
  But no key-reading rule lets a linebacker ignore a man crossing the backfield at full speed who might
  have the ball, so his first steps tend to go with him. Whether or not the receiver gets the ball, the
  defense's whole second level is now moving sideways, which is exactly what the rest of this chapter
  takes advantage of.

The mechanics vary. In some offenses the quarterback hands the ball off in front of himself; in others
(Kansas City's, for one) he flips it forward a foot or two to a receiver passing in front of him, a
"pop" or [shovel](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd) toss that
counts as a forward pass in the record books. The flip has a hidden advantage: if the exchange is
botched, the ball on the ground is an incomplete pass, not a fumble.[^popPass] (It also means those
plays won't appear in the run data later in this chapter.) Either way, the runner is gone before the
defense has finished its first step.

Some offenses go one step further and make the jet an [option](03-04-option-football.qmd). The
quarterback reads a defender on the jet side, usually the end or whoever is responsible for the edge,
exactly as 03-04's read option reads an end: if that defender widens to take the jet, the quarterback
hands the ball inside; if he sits inside, the jet man gets it. The motion man's job is the same either
way, which is why the defense can't tell from his speed or his path.

```{python}
#| label: fig-jet-sweep
#| fig-cap: "A jet sweep left against a nickel defense playing zone (simulated, BDB-format tracking; faint lines are each player's path so far). 1: Z (green ring) sprints across in jet motion; nobody follows him, so the defense is in zone. 2: Z takes the handoff at full speed, and both linebackers (orange rings) are already moving toward him. 3: the linebackers and the nickel back run hard to the jet side; H blocks the nickel and X the cornerback, while the offensive line steps left and engages the defensive linemen. 4: Z is outside and past the linebackers, with the deep safety (FS) coming down as the last man to beat. The shaded area on the right, where the running back (R) faked a run, has no linebacker left in it: that is where the plays later in this chapter attack."
def jet_formation():
    """11 personnel from the gun: X on the line far left, H in the left slot (off the line), the tight end
    attached on the right and Z off the line outside him. Seven on the line: the five linemen, X and Y."""
    return check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.8, "R"),
                                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("H", "WR", OFF_D, -8.5),
                                 O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 12.0)])


def nickel(cb_l=-15.0, cb_r=12.5):
    return front(pe=("9", 5.7), pt=("3", 2.35), bt=("1", -0.7), be=("5", -4.0),
                 lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.8, "M")),
                 extra=(("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.0, "NB"),), cb=(cb_l, cb_r))


def jet_sweep_play():
    p = Play(jet_formation(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=10)
    motion_to(p, "Z", [(-2.8, 7.5)], (-3.0, 2.2), speed=6.5)          # jet motion: ball snapped 2 yd short of Q
    go_to(p, "Z", (13.0, -15.2), "run", speed=9.0,
          via=[(-3.1, -0.5), (-2.6, -6.0), (-0.8, -11.0), (3.0, -13.6), (7.5, -14.6)])
    p.handoff("Z", t=0.3)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-4.4, -0.3), "path", speed=2.5)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.6, 1.2), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.1)          # then carry out a fake
    go_to(p, "RB", (-1.4, 6.6), "path", delay=0.3, speed=5.5, via=[(-4.0, 0.6), (-2.8, 3.8)])  # fake a run right
    # the line steps left (zone steps toward the sweep) and engages the down linemen
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.4, -4.7), via=[(-0.4, -3.9)], speed=2.4)        # reach the 5
    go_to(p, "LG", (1.1, -2.6), via=[(-0.4, -2.0)], speed=2.2)        # step, then climb through the gap
    go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -1.4), via=[(-0.4, -0.8)], speed=2.2)         # reach the 1
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.3, 1.6), speed=1.6)                             # cut off the 3
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.2, 3.5), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 5.1), via=[(-0.5, 4.7)], speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "H", (2.6, -10.4), via=[(-0.6, -9.6)], speed=4.5)        # arc to the nickel
    go_to(p, "X", (4.4, -16.6), speed=4.0, via=[(1.5, -15.4)])         # stalk the corner
    # the defense: the down linemen fight the blocks; the second level flows hard to the jet
    go_to(p, "DE_L", (1.3, -5.3), "path", speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "DT_L", (1.3, -1.9), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "DT_R", (1.2, 1.7), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "DE_R", (1.6, 4.4), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (5.2, -11.2), "path", speed=5.5, via=[(4.0, -5.0), (4.4, -8.6)])
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (5.6, -8.6), "path", speed=5.5, delay=0.05, via=[(4.2, -1.0), (4.6, -5.0)])
    go_to(p, "NB", (3.2, -10.9), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.15)
    go_to(p, "LCB", (5.6, -16.9), "path", speed=2.8, via=[(7.6, -15.6)])
    go_to(p, "FS", (9.6, -13.4), "path", speed=5.0, delay=0.3, via=[(11.0, -10.0)])
    go_to(p, "SS", (10.4, -5.0), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.4, via=[(11.5, 0.0)])
    go_to(p, "RCB", (8.5, 8.8), "path", speed=2.5, delay=0.6)
    return p


def jet_empty(ax, fld, t):
    """Last panel: shade the side the running back faked to, now empty of linebackers."""
    if t < 2.0:
        return
    x0, y0 = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(*JET_PLAY.to_abs(5.0, 4.4)))
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x0, y0), 9.0, 6.4, fc=GREEN, alpha=0.12, ec=GREEN, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.5))
    ax.text(x0, y0 + 1.0, "empty", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=GREEN, fontweight="bold",
            zorder=12)


JET_PLAY = jet_sweep_play()
JET_T = [-1.0, 0.5, 1.3, 2.6]
JET_NOTES = ["Jet motion: Z sprints across;\nnobody follows him (zone)",
             "Handoff at full speed; both\nlinebackers' first steps go with him",
             "Linebackers and nickel fly to the\njet; H and X block on the edge",
             "Z is around the corner. The right\nside, where R faked, is empty"]
animated(JET_PLAY, JET_T, JET_NOTES, lateral=(-19.5, 14.0), window=(-7.0, 13.5),
         rings=(("Z", style.THIRD), ("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("WILL", style.DEFENSE)), decorate=jet_empty)
```

Look at the third and fourth panels of @fig-jet-sweep, not at Z. Five defenders (both linebackers, the
nickel back, the cornerback and the free safety) are all running toward the left sideline, and the
defense's right side is down to two defensive linemen held at the line, a cornerback out wide and a
safety rotating over the top, around grass nobody is using. That is the
jet sweep's second job. Even when it gains four yards, it teaches the defense that the left sideline
is where the danger is, and a defense that has learned that lesson will run there faster next time.

**What it gives up.** The jet sweep is a high-variance play. When the force player holds the edge, the
runner is caught going sideways behind the line, and the loss can be large because he started deep.
The exchange happens at full speed between two players moving in different directions, which adds
fumble risk (the forward flip is one answer). The risk is real but small: over the ten seasons
2016–2025, receivers lost a fumble on about 0.65% of their carries, against 0.46% for running backs, a
difference of roughly one extra lost fumble every 500 carries (course calculation from nflverse
play-by-play; the receivers' figure rests on only 26 lost fumbles). And it uses a receiver as a runner, so every jet sweep is a play on which that receiver
isn't running a route. Coaches accept all of that because of what the motion does to the defense when
the ball goes somewhere else, which is the subject of the rest of the chapter.

## End-arounds and reverses: sending the ball back

If the defense is going to run hard one way, the obvious punishment is to give the ball to someone
running the other way. There are two classic ways to do it, and broadcasters mix up their names all
the time.

An [**end-around**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-end-around) gives the ball to a receiver who comes
back behind the line from his spot outside and runs toward the other side of the field. The quarterback
hands it to him directly: one exchange. Usually the play starts with a fake the opposite way, so the
defense flows toward the fake while the receiver runs away from it. (The name is older than the modern
receiver: the "end" in end-around is the end of the line, the position that became the wide receiver
and the tight end.)

A [**reverse**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-reverse) has two exchanges. The ball first goes to a
player running one way, usually a running back on a sweep, and he hands or pitches it to a teammate
running the other way. The ball's direction *reverses* behind the line. A double reverse does it again.

```{python}
#| label: fig-reverse
#| fig-cap: "Two ways to send the ball back against a defense flowing right (dashed orange arrows). Left, an end-around: the quarterback fakes a handoff to the running back going right, then hands the ball to Z, who came behind the line from his spot on the right and runs left. One exchange (football icon), about four yards deep. Right, a reverse: the quarterback hands off to the back going right, and the back hands the ball to Z coming the other way. Two exchanges, about six yards deep. In both, the play depends on the backside end (ringed). Here he does his job and stays home, so the left tackle has to get outside him and wall him inside, and the quarterback, once the ball is gone, leads up the field for the first defender who turns back."
def reverse_play(kind):
    off = check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.5, 0.0, "R"),
                                O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -11.0), O("H", "WR", OFF_D, -7.0),
                                O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 9.0)])
    dfn = front(pe=("9", 5.7), be=("5", -4.0), lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M")),
                extra=(("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.2, "NB"),), cb=(-11.0, 10.0))
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    if kind == "end-around":
        go_to(p, "QB", (-3.4, 0.6), "path", speed=2.5)                         # fake to the back ...
        go_to(p, "RB", (-1.0, 5.2), "path", speed=6.0, via=[(-5.0, 2.6)])      # ... who runs the fake right
        go_to(p, "Z", (9.0, -11.8), "run", speed=7.5,
              via=[(-3.2, 6.5), (-4.1, 2.0), (-4.2, -2.5), (-3.4, -6.4), (-0.4, -9.4)])
        p.handoff("Z", t=1.1)
        go_to(p, "QB", (2.8, -5.4), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.5, via=[(-2.4, -3.2), (0.4, -4.6)])   # then lead
        swaps = [("QB", 1.1)]
    else:
        go_to(p, "QB", (-4.0, 1.0), "path", speed=4.5)
        p.handoff("RB", t=0.4)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-4.8, 4.6), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-4.6, 1.8)])
        go_to(p, "Z", (8.5, -11.8), "run", speed=7.5,
              via=[(-3.4, 7.0), (-5.0, 5.0), (-5.4, 0.0), (-4.4, -5.8), (-0.4, -9.4)])
        p.handoff("Z", t=0.85)
        go_to(p, "QB", (2.8, -5.4), "path", speed=4.5, delay=0.3, via=[(-2.6, -2.8), (0.4, -4.6)])
        swaps = [("QB", 0.4), ("RB", 0.85)]
    for k, end in (("C", (0.2, 0.8)), ("RG", (0.3, 2.6)), ("RT", (0.3, 4.2)), ("Y", (0.4, 6.0)),
                   ("LG", (0.2, -0.6))):
        go_to(p, k, end)                                                       # the line shows flow right
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.7, -4.6), via=[(-0.6, -3.9)])                            # get outside the end, wall him in
    go_to(p, "X", (5.0, -11.0))                                                # stalk the corner
    go_to(p, "H", (3.8, -8.4))                                                 # block the nickel
    p.highlight("Z")
    return p, swaps


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
for ax, kind, ttl in [(axes[0], "end-around", "End-around: one exchange"),
                      (axes[1], "reverse", "Reverse: two exchanges")]:
    p, swaps = reverse_play(kind)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-14.5, 12.5), window=(-9.6, 12.0), title=False)
    for pts in ([(4.5, -2.6), (3.6, 1.5), (3.0, 4.0)], [(4.5, 1.6), (3.4, 5.4)], [(12.0, -8.0), (9.6, -1.0)],
                [(12.0, 8.0), (8.6, 9.6)]):
        flow(f, p, pts)
    x, y = _P(f, p, 1.0, -4.0)
    ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.25, fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.8, zorder=7))
    for who, t in swaps:                                                       # mark each exchange point
        bx, by = (float(v) for v in _P(f, p, *p.position(who, t)))
        ax.add_patch(Ellipse((bx, by), 1.2, 0.75, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=11))
    if kind == "end-around":
        say(f, p, -6.8, 6.0, "fake", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        point_to(f, p, (-8.2, -3.6), p.position("QB", 1.1), "Q to Z", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
    else:
        point_to(f, p, (-8.0, -3.6), p.position("QB", 0.4), "1st: Q to R", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        point_to(f, p, (-8.2, 7.0), p.position("RB", 0.85), "2nd: R to Z", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
    say(f, p, 7.8, 2.2, "defense flows right", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Both plays bet on the same thing: that the defense will chase the first action hard enough to leave
the other side empty. Both are beaten by the same defender, the end on the *backside* (the side away
from the first action). He is the contain player on that side, and his rule in most defenses is not to
chase flat down the line after the fake. He shuffles along behind the line at about the depth of the
ball, trailing the play, and checks the three things that can come back his way before he commits:
a bootleg, a counter, a reverse.[^backside] If he stays home like that, the reverse runs straight into
him six yards behind the line of scrimmage. So the offense has to account for him. In @fig-reverse the
left tackle's job is to get outside him and wall him inside, and the quarterback, once the ball is gone,
leads up the field for the first pursuer who turns back. It is one of the few plays on which a
quarterback is asked to block at all, and most coaches ask only that he get in the way of somebody.

They are also rare. The NFL's play-by-play descriptions mention a reverse on only about 60 runs in the
ten regular seasons 2016–2025, and on just one each in 2023 and 2024. Scorers don't always note a
reverse, so treat those counts as a floor, but the trend is real enough. Those flagged runs averaged
about eight and a half yards (course calculation), which is the pattern this chapter ends on: a play
that pays well *because* it's called only when the defense has been caught chasing.

**When you see one**, ask two questions. Which defender was responsible for the backside, and did he
chase? And how deep was the exchange? A reverse handed off seven yards behind the line has to gain
seven yards just to get back to zero. It's a play for a defense that has been caught chasing on film,
not a play to run every week.

## The Wing-T: an order of football

Most of the ideas in this chapter were organized into a system long before the NFL adopted them. The
[Wing-T](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd), the formation with a wingback
just outside and behind the tight end, was built by Dave Nelson at Maine and then the University of
Delaware, where he coached from 1951 to 1965. His assistant Harold "Tubby" Raymond succeeded him and
ran it for 36 more seasons, until 2001, winning 300 games, a total few coaches have reached at one
school.[^raymond] Raymond, a Michigan graduate famous for painting a portrait of each of his senior players, and
his assistant Ted Kempski wrote the book on it, and the title says what it is about: *The Delaware
Wing-T: An Order of Football*.[^orderbook]

The problem Nelson is usually said to have faced is the one every underdog coach faces: his players were usually not bigger
or faster than the other team's. He couldn't win by blocking every defender one-on-one, so he built an
offense that made defenders block *themselves*, by running to the wrong place.

### The buck sweep

The Wing-T's signature play is the [**buck sweep**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-buck-sweep). Its
name tells you its two halves: the fullback fakes the *buck* (an old word for a straight plunge up the
middle) and the halfback runs the *sweep*.

```{python}
#| label: fig-buck-sweep
#| fig-cap: "The Wing-T buck sweep, right (wingback W outside the tight end Y; halfback H behind the left tackle; fullback F behind the quarterback; split end X on the left). Everything on the play side blocks down: the wingback on the end, Y on the Sam, the right tackle on the 3-technique. Both guards pull (purple rings): the right guard kicks out the first defender outside the wingback's block (here the cornerback, who comes up to force), and the left guard turns up inside him to block a linebacker. The center blocks back into the hole the left guard left, and the fullback fakes the buck into the gap the right guard left. The halfback takes a reverse-pivot handoff and follows the guards; the quarterback fakes a bootleg the other way."
def wing_t():
    """The Wing-T: Q under center, F behind him, H behind the left tackle, W just outside and behind Y,
    X split on the left. Seven on the line: five linemen, X and Y."""
    return check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0.0, "F"),
                                 O("HB", "RB", -4.5, -3.2, "H"), O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8),
                                 O("W", "WR", -1.6, 6.5, "W"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -12.0)])


def wing_t_d():
    return front(pe=("9", 5.7), pt=("3", 2.35), bt=("1", -0.7), be=("5", -4.0),
                 lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.3, "M"), ("SAM", 4.3, 4.6, "S")),
                 cb=(-12.0, 10.0), safeties=((13.0, -1.0), (8.5, 10.4)))


p = Play(wing_t(), wing_t_d(), los=35, to_go=10, title="Buck sweep right")
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.8, -0.9), "path", speed=3.0)                                  # reverse pivot
go_to(p, "QB", (-5.4, -7.6), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.25, via=[(-3.0, -1.6), (-3.6, -4.8)])  # fake a boot
p.handoff("HB", t=0.8)
go_to(p, "HB", (12.5, 8.2), "run", via=[(-5.4, -1.0), (-5.6, 3.0), (-4.6, 6.6), (-2.6, 8.4), (1.4, 8.6)])
go_to(p, "FB", (-1.0, 1.0), "path", via=[(-2.6, 0.9)])                           # fake the buck, fill
p.block("W", target="DE_R"); p.block("Y", target="SAM"); p.block("RT", target="DT_R")
go_to(p, "RG", (4.8, 9.6), "pull", via=[(-1.9, 2.6), (-2.5, 6.0), (-1.2, 8.6)])   # kick out the force
go_to(p, "LG", (3.0, 6.6), "pull", via=[(-2.9, -0.7), (-3.2, 4.4), (-2.4, 7.0), (0.6, 7.6)])  # turn up inside
go_to(p, "C", (0.2, -1.0), via=[(-0.4, -0.6)])                                   # block back
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -3.4), via=[(-0.6, -3.8)])                                  # cut off
go_to(p, "X", (8.0, -12.0), "route")
p.highlight("HB"); p.highlight("RG", color=PURPLE); p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-14.5, 16.0), window=(-10.0, 14.0))
flow(fld, p, [(6.5, 10.0), (5.4, 9.9)], lw=1.3)                                  # the corner comes up
flow(fld, p, [(4.5, 1.3), (4.0, 3.0), (3.5, 6.2)], lw=1.3)                       # the Mike scrapes
point_to(fld, p, (1.4, 13.0), (4.6, 9.8), "kick-out", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(fld, p, (8.8, 0.6), (3.0, 6.6), "LG turns up\non the Mike", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -7.9, -8.0, "Q: fake\nthe boot", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

The buck sweep is power football, the same family as the [gap schemes](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)
of 03-03: down blocks to wall off the inside, pullers to add blockers at the point of attack. It is
also a close relative of the most famous run in NFL history, Vince Lombardi's Packers sweep of the
1960s, which also pulled both guards around a down-blocking line, and an ancestor of today's
[pin-and-pull](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd).

What makes it a Wing-T play rather than just a sweep is everything that happens in the backfield
*before* the ball goes outside. In the first second the defense sees the fullback plunge at the middle,
the quarterback spin with his back to the line, the halfback run across, and both guards pull. Then, a
beat later, the quarterback rolls the other way without the ball. A linebacker who reads the fullback
steps up; one who reads the guards flies outside; one who reads the quarterback drifts backside. Only
one of them is right.

### Series football: every play is the answer to the last one

That first second is the point. Raymond's Wing-T was built as
[**series football**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-series-football): groups of plays that begin with
the *same* backfield action and end differently, each one designed to beat the defense's reaction to
another. Chris Brown, writing about Raymond's influence, put the idea in one line: "each time a team
tries to stop one thing, it opens itself up to something else."[^brown] The buck series is the
classic example.

```{python}
#| label: fig-buck-series
#| fig-cap: "The buck series as a conversation. Every play starts with the same first second (blue box, left). Each orange arrow is something the defense might do to stop the buck sweep, and the box it leads to is the play in the series that punishes that reaction. The plays are illustrative of the Wing-T's logic; real playbooks have more members and different names."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 66); ax.axis("off")


def box(x, y, w, h, title, body, ec, fc, title_fs=8.4, gap=6.4):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - w / 2, y - h / 2), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.4,rounding_size=1.4",
                                fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=1.3, zorder=2))
    ax.text(x - w / 2 + 2, y + h / 2 - 2.0, title, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=title_fs, fontweight="bold",
            color=style.INK, zorder=3)
    ax.text(x - w / 2 + 2, y + h / 2 - gap, body, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK_2,
            zorder=3, linespacing=1.2)


box(15, 31, 27, 30, "Buck sweep\n(the base play)", "F fakes up the\nmiddle; both guards\npull; H sweeps\nbehind them; Q\nfakes the boot away",
    style.OFFENSE, style.OFFENSE_TINT, title_fs=8.6, gap=10.0)
rows = [(54.5, "Buck trap", "F keeps it up the middle; a guard traps\nthe lineman left unblocked", "linebackers run\nwith the guards"),
        (39.0, "Waggle", "Q keeps it and boots away behind a\npulling guard: run or throw", "backside end\nchases the sweep"),
        (23.5, "Counter or reverse", "W comes back the other way,\nagainst the flow", "whole defense\nflows to the sweep"),
        (8.0, "Play-action deep", "same fake; the ends run past the\nsafety who came up to stop it", "a safety flies up\nto force")]
for y, title, body, why in rows:
    box(78, y, 42, 12.5, title, body, GREEN, style.SURFACE)
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((29.5, 31 + (y - 31) * 0.35), (56.0, y), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11,
                                 color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, zorder=1))
    ax.text(43.5, 31 + (y - 31) * 0.68 + 2.6, why, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.6,
            color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, style="italic", zorder=3, linespacing=1.15,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
ax.text(43.5, 64, "if the defense...", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
ax.text(78, 64, "...the series answers with", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color=GREEN)
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-buck-series from left to right. If the linebackers learn to fly outside with the pulling
guards, the fullback, who faked into the middle on the sweep, keeps the ball this time, and the middle
they just vacated is where he runs: the **buck trap**, a [trap](03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd) in which
the defensive lineman left unblocked at the snap gets hit from the side by a pulling guard. If the
backside end chases the sweep, the quarterback keeps the ball and rolls out behind him. If the whole
defense flows, the wingback comes back the other way on a counter or reverse. If a safety races up to
make the tackle on the sweep, the receivers run past him on
[play-action](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) (a fake handoff followed by a pass).

None of those plays is clever on its own. A trap is a trap. What makes the series work is that each
play is *indistinguishable from the others for the first second*, and that the defender's correct
reaction to one is his wrong reaction to another. The defense can't stop all of them by being fast or
by being patient; it has to be right, play after play, about a fake it can't see through. That is what
"an order of football" means: plays called in a deliberate order, each one asking the defense a
question the previous one made it answer.

### The waggle

One member of the series reaches straight into the modern NFL. The
[**waggle**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-waggle) is the Wing-T's play-action bootleg: the
quarterback fakes the buck sweep (or another run) one way and rolls out the other, behind a guard who
pulls to that side to protect him, with receivers spread at three depths on that side.

```{python}
#| label: fig-waggle
#| fig-cap: "The waggle, from the same Wing-T look and the same first second as the buck sweep. The halfback and fullback carry out their fakes to the right, and the linebackers flow with them (dashed orange). The quarterback keeps the ball and rolls left. The left guard pulls left to block the backside end (ringed), who has chased the fake inside. The quarterback has three receivers on his side at three depths: the fullback slipping into the flat after his fake, the tight end Y on a deep crossing route from the other side, and the split end X running deep to clear the cornerback away. If nobody comes up to stop him, he runs."
p = Play(wing_t(), wing_t_d(), los=35, to_go=10, title="Waggle left")
go_to(p, "QB", (-2.8, -0.9), "path", speed=3.0)
go_to(p, "QB", (-4.6, -10.4), "run", speed=5.0, delay=0.35, via=[(-4.0, -1.6), (-5.8, -2.6), (-5.6, -6.0)])
go_to(p, "HB", (-3.0, 7.0), "path", via=[(-5.4, -1.0), (-5.0, 3.2)])            # fake the sweep
go_to(p, "FB", (0.0, -8.8), "route", via=[(-2.6, 0.9), (-2.7, -0.8), (-2.8, -5.0)])  # fake the buck, then the flat
go_to(p, "LG", (0.2, -4.6), "pull", via=[(-1.6, -2.4), (-1.6, -4.6)])             # pull to the boot side
go_to(p, "Y", (13.0, -9.0), "route", via=[(5.0, 4.0)])                           # deep crosser
go_to(p, "X", (18.5, -12.4), "route")                                            # clear out deep
go_to(p, "W", (2.0, 4.0), via=[(-1.0, 5.8)])
for k, end in (("C", (0.2, 0.8)), ("RG", (0.3, 2.6)), ("RT", (0.3, 4.1)), ("LT", (0.2, -2.2))):
    go_to(p, k, end)
p.highlight("QB")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-16.0, 13.0), window=(-11.0, 20.5))
flow(fld, p, [(1.0, -4.0), (0.6, -3.0)], lw=1.3)
x, y = _P(fld, p, 1.0, -4.0)
fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 1.25, fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.8, zorder=7))
for pts in ([(4.5, -2.6), (3.8, 0.4)], [(4.5, 1.3), (3.6, 4.6)], [(4.3, 4.6), (3.6, 6.6)]):
    flow(fld, p, pts, lw=1.3)
say(fld, p, -2.6, 9.6, "the sweep fake", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 1.0, -10.8, "flat", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 13.8, -5.0, "deep cross", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 17.4, -9.6, "clear", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -8.6, -9.4, "Q: run\nor throw", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

If that picture looks familiar, it should. Replace the Wing-T backfield with a single back running
[outside zone](03-02-zone-running.qmd) and you have the bootleg that Mike Shanahan's and Kyle Shanahan's
offenses, and Sean McVay's, built on (taught in full in
[Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd), where
the version with no pulling guard at all, the *naked* bootleg, gets its own treatment). The waggle's
idea, fake hard one way and put the quarterback on the edge the other way with three receivers at three
depths, survived when the formation that invented it disappeared.

## The Wing-T's children

You will almost never see a true Wing-T in the NFL. You will see its children every Sunday.

**The jet sweep.** Wing-T offenses already sent the wingback in motion, and the *fly sweep*, a
handoff to a wingback or slot in full-speed motion behind an under-center quarterback, grew up beside
them. Its exact origin is murky: many coaches credit Gene Beck's Delano High School teams in California
in the 1950s. In the 1980s and 1990s coaches such as Mark Speckman built whole offenses around it, with
a trap, a bootleg and passes off the same motion, and spread it through high school clinics; Dan
Hawkins carried it from small-college Willamette to Boise State, where it helped launch the Broncos'
run of winning offenses in 1999 and 2000.[^fly] Many Wing-T coaches adopted it, and the two are now
usually taught together.
Move the quarterback back to the shotgun, call the motion "jet," and you have the NFL play. Pro Football Focus counted 174 jet sweep
runs across the league in 2017 and 309 in 2018, when they averaged 6.1 yards a carry and Sean McVay's
Rams ran 48 of them, playoffs included.[^pffjet]

**Gus Malzahn's Auburn.** The clearest line from Delaware to modern football runs through Gus Malzahn.
As a young high school coach in Arkansas in the early 1990s, he taught himself offense from Raymond
and Kempski's book; by the late 1990s he had moved to an up-tempo shotgun spread, but kept the
Wing-T's plays and its series logic, and at Auburn he ran the buck sweep from the shotgun with pulling
linemen and a receiver faking an end-around the other way.[^brownmalzahn] His 2013 team averaged more
than 300 rushing yards a game, the first SEC team to do it in almost thirty years.

**The NFL's misdirection revival.** When the McVay Rams and Kyle Shanahan's 49ers made jet motion a
weekly staple in the late 2010s, they were doing what Raymond did with his backfield: one
picture, several plays. Shanahan went a step further with Deebo Samuel, a receiver he lined up in the
backfield, put in motion and handed the ball on sweeps, reverses and runs between the tackles, so that
"which player is the runner" became one more question the defense had to get right. Andy Reid's Chiefs
used jet and orbit motion to set up flips, shovels and screens back the other way. The formations are
modern; the logic is the Wing-T's.

## Eye candy: half a second is a gap

Here is the payoff from @fig-jet-sweep. Once the defense has learned to fly at jet motion, the motion
itself becomes a weapon even when the ball goes somewhere else. Coaches call this
[**eye candy**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-eye-candy): motion and fakes by players who won't get
the ball, designed to pull defenders' eyes and first steps the wrong way.

How much can a fake buy? Not much, and that's enough. A linebacker who takes one hard step toward a jet
fake and then has to come back has lost about half a second. Linebackers move at something like 5 to 7
yards a second when they're trying to fill a hole; half a second is three yards. A hole on an inside
run is a yard or two wide and stays open for less than a second. A linebacker three yards out of place
doesn't fill it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-eye-candy
#| fig-cap: "Eye candy: a jet fake left, an inside zone run right (simulated, BDB-format tracking). The dashed outline is where the Mike linebacker would be at the same moment if there had been no jet motion and he had simply read the run (a second simulation of the same play without the motion). 1: Z in jet motion; every defender's eyes go to him. 2: at half a second the quarterback has faked to Z and is handing to R. The Mike (ringed) took his first step toward the jet; without the fake he would already be filling the hole. 3: the right guard climbs to the Mike, who is only now coming back. 4: the back is through the hole. The backside end (5) also widened for the jet, so he is too far away to chase the back from behind."
def eye_candy_play(jet=True):
    p = Play(jet_formation(), front(pe=("7", 4.0), pt=("1", 0.7), bt=("3", -2.35), be=("5", -4.0),
                                    lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.2, "M")),
                                    extra=(("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.0, "NB"),), cb=(-15.0, 12.5)),
             los=35, to_go=10)
    if jet:
        motion_to(p, "Z", [(-2.8, 7.5)], (-3.0, 2.2), speed=6.5)
        go_to(p, "Z", (2.0, -15.5), "path", speed=8.0, via=[(-3.1, -0.5), (-2.6, -6.0), (-1.0, -11.0)])
        go_to(p, "QB", (-4.5, -0.6), "path", speed=2.4)                 # ride the fake to Z ...
        go_to(p, "QB", (-4.9, -0.1), "path", speed=2.0)                 # ... then turn to hand off
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.3, -0.6), "path", speed=3.6)                # first step: toward the jet
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.7, 1.5), "path", speed=4.6)                 # then back to the run, late
        go_to(p, "WILL", (4.3, -4.6), "path", speed=3.6)
        go_to(p, "WILL", (3.6, -1.0), "path", speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "DE_L", (1.3, -5.6), "path", speed=1.6)                # widens to respect the jet
        go_to(p, "NB", (3.6, -10.2), "path", speed=3.5)
        go_to(p, "FS", (10.0, -10.5), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.2)
    else:
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.5, 2.4), "path", speed=5.2)                 # no fake: he reads the run and fills
        go_to(p, "WILL", (3.2, -0.5), "path", speed=4.5)
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.6)
    go_to(p, "RB", (10.5, 3.8), "run", delay=0.15, speed=6.5,
          via=[(-4.6, -0.4), (-2.6, 1.8), (0.4, 3.0), (5.0, 3.7)])
    # inside zone right: the double teams and the climbs (03-02)
    go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.6), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "DT_R", (1.5, 0.3), "path", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "RG", (3.0, 1.1), via=[(-0.2, 1.1), (0.3, 1.2)], speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.6, 3.8), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "DE_R", (1.6, 4.2), "path", speed=0.9)
    go_to(p, "Y", (3.6, 6.2), via=[(-0.2, 4.4), (0.4, 4.6)], speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.5, -2.6), speed=2.0); go_to(p, "DT_L", (1.4, -2.4), "path", speed=0.9)
    go_to(p, "LG", (3.3, -1.3), via=[(-0.2, -1.9), (0.3, -2.0)], speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "H", (2.4, -9.8), speed=3.5)
    go_to(p, "X", (10.0, -15.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "SS", (9.0, 4.0), "path", speed=3.5, delay=0.5)
    return p


EYE_T = [-0.9, 0.5, 1.0, 2.2]
EYE_NOTES = ["Jet motion: every defender's\neyes go to Z",
             "Jet fake. The Mike stepped toward Z;\ndashed outline: where he'd be without it",
             "The guard climbs to the Mike,\nwho is only now coming back",
             "R is through the hole; the end (5)\nwidened for the jet and can't chase"]
animated(eye_candy_play(True), EYE_T, EYE_NOTES, lateral=(-11.5, 10.5), window=(-7.0, 10.5),
         rings=(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("RB", style.THIRD)), ghosts=(eye_candy_play(False), ["MIKE"]))
```

Two defenders were taken out of @fig-eye-candy without being blocked. The Mike linebacker's first
step went the wrong way, so the guard who climbed to him got there in time. And the backside end, who
on a normal inside zone run is the unblocked defender who can chase the back down from behind (03-02
spent a whole section on him), widened to protect against the jet sweep, so he was out of the play. One
receiver running across the formation did the work of two blockers.

That is the trade eye candy makes. The receiver in motion isn't blocking anybody, so the offense
starts a man short at the point of attack, and the motion has to hold *more* than one defender for the
play to come out ahead. It usually does only when the defense believes the motion. **Eye candy is only
as good as the last time the ball actually went there.** Robert Woods, one of the 2018 Rams' two main
jet-sweep runners, carried the ball only 19 times in the regular season,[^woods] but the Rams faked the jet
constantly; the defense had to treat every fake as real because some of them weren't.

Jet motion is the most common kind of eye candy, not the only one. An orbit motion behind the
quarterback, a running back faking a sweep one way while the ball goes the other, a tight end running
across the formation as though he's going to block, the quarterback carrying out a bootleg fake after
he hands the ball off: all of them are designed to make a linebacker's eyes and feet do something
for a fraction of a second that they shouldn't.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The jet motion was wasted; the guy didn't even get the ball." On most plays with jet motion the
ball goes to someone else, by design. Judge the motion by what the defenders near it did. If two
linebackers took a step toward the motion man and the run went through the gap one of them left, the
motion was the most important "block" on the play.
:::

## How defenses fight back

None of this is free for the offense, because good defenses train against every trick in this chapter.

- **Keep the backside honest.** The backside end and the backside cornerback have rules on outside
  runs, and the first rule is "don't chase until the ball has crossed the formation." That kills
  reverses and end-arounds and makes bootlegs and waggles harder, at the price of one fewer defender
  pursuing the play that really does go outside.
- **Answer the crack.** When a receiver cracks inside, the cornerback over him yells "crack!" and
  steps up to replace the man who was cracked as the force player. The puller then has nobody to block,
  and the back is running at a cornerback who is already outside him.
- **Spin to the motion.** Rotating a safety down toward the jet side at the snap (the *spin* of 02-06)
  puts an extra defender at the edge, so the linebackers don't have to chase. The offense's counter is
  to run the other way, into the side the safety left.
- **Read your keys, not the motion.** Linebackers are taught to read the linemen in front of them
  (their *keys*, which [05-04](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd)
  covers), not the receiver in motion. A guard stepping right means the run is going right, whatever the
  jet man is doing. The problem is that the jet man is going *very fast*, and a linebacker who ignores him
  entirely gets beaten to the edge.

That last point is the defense's version of the dilemma in @fig-edge-dilemma. Every answer that stops
misdirection makes the defense slower to the perimeter, and every answer that stops the perimeter run
makes it more vulnerable to misdirection. The full catalog of run fits, including who forces and who
spills, is in [Run Fits](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).

## Constraint plays: why you can't just run it more

Here is a puzzle in the numbers. When an NFL wide receiver carries the ball on a run, almost always on
a jet sweep, an end-around or a reverse, the play works much better on average than a running back's
carry. So why do teams hand it to receivers less than once a game?

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (load 2016-2025 runs and tag the ball carrier's position)"
#| output: false
from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

YEARS = list(range(2016, 2026))
runs = pbp(YEARS, columns=["season", "season_type", "play_type", "rusher_player_id", "epa", "success",
                           "yards_gained", "qb_kneel", "down", "game_id", "posteam"])
runs = runs[(runs["season_type"] == "REG") & (runs["play_type"] == "run") & (runs["qb_kneel"] == 0)
            & runs["down"].notna()]
rosters = nfl().load_rosters(YEARS).to_pandas()[["season", "gsis_id", "position"]]
rosters = rosters.drop_duplicates(["season", "gsis_id"])
runs = runs.merge(rosters, left_on=["season", "rusher_player_id"], right_on=["season", "gsis_id"], how="left")
rb_wr = runs[runs["position"].isin(["RB", "WR"])]
by_season = rb_wr.groupby(["season", "position"])["epa"].mean().unstack()
team_games = runs.groupby("season")["game_id"].nunique() * 2
wr_per_game = rb_wr[rb_wr["position"] == "WR"].groupby("season").size() / team_games
profile = rb_wr.groupby("position").agg(
    carries=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"), success=("success", "mean"),
    lost=("yards_gained", lambda s: (s < 0).mean()), big=("yards_gained", lambda s: (s >= 10).mean()))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# guard the numbers quoted in the text against a data refresh
assert abs(profile.loc["WR", "epa"] - 0.10) < 0.02 and abs(profile.loc["RB", "epa"] + 0.07) < 0.02
assert abs(profile.loc["WR", "success"] - 0.51) < 0.02 and abs(profile.loc["RB", "success"] - 0.39) < 0.02
assert abs(profile.loc["WR", "lost"] - 0.15) < 0.02 and abs(profile.loc["RB", "lost"] - 0.10) < 0.02
assert abs(profile.loc["WR", "big"] - 0.22) < 0.02 and abs(profile.loc["RB", "big"] - 0.10) < 0.02
assert wr_per_game.max() < 0.95 and wr_per_game.min() > 0.55
assert (by_season["WR"] > by_season["RB"]).all()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-wr-runs
#| fig-cap: "Wide receivers as runners, NFL regular seasons 2016–2025. Left: expected points added (EPA) per carry by the ball carrier's position. A running back's average carry loses a little expected value every season; a wide receiver's is worth more than a running back's in every season, and is positive in eight of the ten. Right: the shape of the outcomes, all ten seasons pooled. Receiver runs are more often successful and twice as often go for 10 or more yards, but they also lose yards more often. League-wide there were only 0.6 to 0.9 receiver carries per team per game. Runs only (jet flips scored as forward passes are not included); kneel-downs removed; position from nflverse season rosters. Data: nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy; course calculation."
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.0), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.35, 1]})
WR_C, RB_C = style.OFFENSE, style.MUTED
a1.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, zorder=1)
```
