```{python}
for pos, col, lab in (("WR", WR_C, "Wide receivers"), ("RB", RB_C, "Running backs")):
    a1.plot(by_season.index, by_season[pos], color=col, lw=2, marker="o", ms=4.5, mec=style.SURFACE, mew=1.2)
    a1.text(2025.35, by_season[pos].iloc[-1], lab, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.5, va="center", ha="left")
a1.set_xlim(2015.5, 2028.6)
a1.set_xticks([2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024])
a1.set_ylabel("EPA per carry", fontsize=8)
a1.set_title("Value per carry, by season", fontsize=9)
a1.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
labels = ["Lost yards", "Successful (EPA > 0)", "Gained 10+ yards"]
cols = ["lost", "success", "big"]
yy = np.arange(len(cols))
for off_, pos, col in ((-0.19, "WR", WR_C), (0.19, "RB", RB_C)):
    vals = profile.loc[pos, cols].values * 100
    a2.barh(yy + off_, vals, height=0.36, color=col, edgecolor=style.SURFACE, linewidth=1.5)
    for y_, v in zip(yy + off_, vals):
        a2.text(v + 1.0, y_, f"{v:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK_2)
a2.set_yticks(yy, labels, fontsize=7.5)
a2.invert_yaxis()
a2.set_xlim(0, 64)
a2.set_xlabel("share of carries (%)", fontsize=8)
a2.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
a2.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
a2.set_title("Outcomes, 2016–2025", fontsize=9)
fig.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], color=WR_C, lw=6, label="Wide receivers"),
                    Line2D([], [], color=RB_C, lw=6, label="Running backs")],
           loc="lower center", ncol=2, fontsize=7.5, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02), frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 1), w_pad=1.5)
plt.show()
```

The numbers in @fig-wr-runs are striking. Across ten seasons, a running back's carry was worth about
**−0.07** expected points on average and succeeded (gained expected points) 39% of the time. A
receiver's carry was worth about **+0.10** and succeeded 51% of the time, and it gained ten or more
yards on 22% of carries, more than twice the running backs' rate. If you have read
[13-02](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd), you'll know that a gap of
0.17 expected points a play is enormous. It's roughly the gap between a good passing play and a bad
run.

But notice the other bar: receivers *lose* yards on 15% of their carries, against 10% for backs. That
is the jet sweep and reverse caught behind the line. And notice the volume: well under one receiver
carry per team per game, every season. Teams aren't ignoring free yards. The yards come *from* the
rarity.

Coaches call plays like these [**constraint plays**](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd),
plays whose main job is to punish the defense for overplaying the offense's *base* plays, the bread-and-butter
runs and passes it calls most. The idea is developed fully in
[Constraint Theory](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd), but the shape is
already visible here. A jet sweep gains a lot when the defense isn't ready for it, and the defense
isn't ready for it because the offense mostly runs something else. Run it twenty times a game and the
defense would stop playing the inside run and start sitting on the edge, the jet sweep would turn into a
two-yard loss, and the inside run would get worse too, because the linebackers would no longer be
taking those hard first steps toward the motion. The value of a misdirection play lives partly in
the plays it *isn't*.

The same caution applies when you read the chart. Some of the receivers' edge is selection: coaches
call these plays when the film says the defense is vulnerable to them, and the defense often isn't
expecting a receiver run at all. That is not a flaw in the numbers; it's the point. A constraint play's
average looks great *because* it's called at the right moments.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Misdirection exists because pursuit works. A defense that runs to the ball fast and together is the
best answer to almost every run in football, so the offense needs plays that make running fast to the
ball a mistake: plays that go back the other way (reverses, counters, waggles) and motion that makes the
defense run to the wrong place (eye candy). The price is risk and blockers: misdirection plays lose
yards more often, take longer to develop, and use players as decoys who could have been blocking. They
work only in the right dose, which is why the best offenses build them into series, so the base play and
its answers look the same until it's too late.
:::

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Delaware, 1966-2001 (Tubby Raymond's Wing-T)"}
There is no tracking data for Raymond's Delaware teams, and you don't need it. If you can find old
Blue Hens film, watch the backfield and not the ball for the first second of any play: the fullback
plunging, the quarterback spinning with his back to the line, the halfback crossing, both guards
pulling. Then watch the linebackers. On the buck sweep they are a step slow to the outside because
the fullback's fake made them look inside first; on the trap and the waggle they are a step out of the
middle because the sweep has been killing them. The plays changed little for decades. Delaware kept
winning with them because the defense's problem never went away: a defense has to react to *something*,
and everything it can react to is a fake on most plays.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Auburn 2013 (Gus Malzahn)"}
Malzahn's 2013 Auburn team, led by quarterback Nick Marshall and running back Tre Mason, ran for more
than 300 yards a game and reached the national championship game. What to notice: the buck sweep from
the shotgun. The guards pull exactly as in @fig-buck-sweep, but the quarterback is five yards deep and
the "halfback" is lined up beside him. A receiver often runs across the backfield the other way, faking
the end-around, the Wing-T's buck fake moved to a different player. And the series is there too: the
same look produces the sweep, an inside run and a quarterback keep.[^auburn]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2018 (Sean McVay)"}
The 2018 Rams made the jet sweep an NFL staple: PFF counted 48 of them, playoffs included, twice as
many as any other team.[^pffjet2] In the nflverse play-by-play, Rams wide receivers carried the ball 35
times in the regular season, and those carries averaged about +0.44 expected points, among the best in
the league that year (course calculation). The two counts differ because a charting service tags the
*play*, while play-by-play records who carried the ball, and some jet plays are scored as passes.
What to notice: the jet sweep is blocked like [outside zone](03-02-zone-running.qmd), the whole line
stepping toward the sweep, so for the first second it looks exactly like the Rams' base run going the
same direction. Then watch the next play with the same motion: half the time the ball goes the other
way, or the quarterback fakes it and throws.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers, Super Bowl LIV (2019 season)"}
Deebo Samuel was a rookie receiver in 2019 who ran the ball 14 times for 159 yards and three
touchdowns in the regular season.[^deebo] In Super Bowl LIV against Kansas City he carried three times
for 53 yards, two of them gains of 32 and 14 yards around the ends, at the time the most rushing yards
by a wide receiver in a Super Bowl.[^deebosb]
What to notice: the 49ers didn't hide that Samuel might get the ball. They moved him around so the
defense had to decide, on every snap, whether the receiver crossing the formation was a decoy. When
linebackers stayed home to stop the inside run, he got the ball at the edge; when they chased him, the
49ers ran Raheem Mostert inside. By 2021, as [02-06](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)
showed, Samuel was effectively a second running back.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Watch the second level.** On every play with jet or orbit motion:

*Before the snap*

- Find the motion man and the side he's heading to. Does anyone travel with him (man coverage), does
  everyone slide a spot (zone), or does a safety spin down toward his side?
- Find the two linebackers and the backside end. These are the players whose reaction you'll grade.

*At the snap: forget the ball for one second*

- Watch the linebackers' eyes and feet. Did they take a step toward the motion? Did they keep going?
- Did the backside end squeeze down the line, or stay home?

*After the play*

- Where did the ball go? If it went *with* the motion: did the force player hold the edge, or did
  the runner beat him? Was there a crack block on the edge?
- If it went *away* from the motion: were the linebackers late because they chased? That's eye candy
  working.
- If the defense has been chasing all game, start expecting the play that goes back the other way: a
  counter, a reverse, a bootleg.

For your prediction log ([01-06](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)): on every jet
motion, write **G** (the motion man gets it) or **F** (fake) before the snap, then **C** if the
linebackers chased, **H** if they held. After a game you'll have a small table of what this defense does
with motion, which is exactly what offensive coordinators study during the week.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1.** First-and-10, ball on the offense's own 35. The offense has run three jet sweeps to the
left today, for 9, 12 and 7 yards. Here Z goes in jet motion again, right to left. This time, as he
crosses, the strong safety (SS, ringed) comes down hard toward the left edge and the free safety slides
to the middle of the field. The two linebackers (W and M) don't move. Should the quarterback give Z the
jet sweep? If not, where would you expect the ball to go?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1, at the snap. Z (green ring) is in jet motion from the right (dashed blue path). The strong safety (SS, ringed) has rotated down toward the left edge and the free safety has moved to the deep middle; hollow outlines show where they started. The linebackers (W, M) haven't moved."
p = Play(jet_formation(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: jet motion, safety spins down")
p.players["Z"] = p.players["Z"].moved(d=-3.0, w=2.2)
p.players["SS"] = p.players["SS"].moved(d=6.0, w=-11.5)
p.players["FS"] = p.players["FS"].moved(d=13.0, w=0.0)
p.highlight("Z", color=style.THIRD); p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 15.0), window=(-8.0, 15.5))
dashed(fld, p, [(-1.5, 12.0), (-2.8, 7.5), (-3.0, 3.3)])
ghost(fld, p, 12.0, 8.0, "SS"); ghost(fld, p, 12.0, -8.0, "FS")
flow(fld, p, [(11.5, 7.0), (6.9, -10.6)], lw=1.2)
flow(fld, p, [(12.0, -7.0), (12.9, -1.1)], lw=1.2)
say(fld, p, 2.6, 9.6, "jet motion", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 9.0, -14.6, "safety spins\nto the edge", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**No jet sweep, probably a run the other way (or play-action).** The safety's spin has done the job
the linebackers usually do: the defense now has an extra player at the left edge before the play
starts, so the jet sweep would run into the cornerback, the nickel *and* a safety coming downhill.
Meanwhile the linebackers stayed home, so a fake to the jet won't move them either. The space is on the
**right**, the side the strong safety just left: one deep safety in the middle, and nobody near the
right edge except a cornerback. Expect the running back on an outside run to the right, a run with the
tight end leading on that side, or a play-action pass behind where the safety used to be.

Compare this with the jet drill in [02-06](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd),
where the linebackers didn't move and *nobody* replaced them at the edge, so the jet was the right
answer. Same linebackers, different safety, opposite call. Many offenses let the quarterback choose
between the jet and the inside run at the snap from exactly this read.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2.** Second-and-4. The offense is in the Wing-T and has run the buck sweep right twice in a row
from this look. Both times, at the snap, the Mike and Will linebackers (ringed) ran hard to the right with
the pulling guards (their paths from those plays are shown in orange). The offense lines up in the same
formation again. What does series football call now, and why?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: the Wing-T look again (wingback W outside the tight end on the right, halfback H behind the left tackle, fullback F behind the quarterback). Dashed orange arrows show where the two linebackers (ringed) ran on the last two buck sweeps, as soon as they saw the guards pull."
p = Play(wing_t(), wing_t_d(), los=35, to_go=4, title="Drill 2: same look, third time")
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE); p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-14.5, 14.5), window=(-7.0, 15.0))
flow(fld, p, [(4.5, 1.3), (5.7, 4.4), (5.0, 8.2)], lw=1.4)
flow(fld, p, [(4.5, -2.6), (3.3, 0.2), (3.0, 3.8)], lw=1.4)
say(fld, p, 8.2, 5.6, "last two plays: the\nlinebackers flew to\nthe pulling guards", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
    fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The buck trap: the fullback keeps the ball up the middle.** The first second will look the same as
the sweep: quarterback reverse-pivots, halfback runs across, the fullback heads for the middle. But this
time the fullback has the ball, and the linemen block for an inside run. A defensive lineman is left
unblocked at the snap and a guard pulls a short distance to trap him (hit him from the side), so the
fullback runs through the gap where that lineman *was*, straight into the space the two linebackers are
about to vacate by chasing the guards. The more the linebackers trust what they saw on the last two
plays, the bigger the hole.

Why not something else? The waggle punishes the *backside end* for chasing, and the drill told you
about the linebackers. A reverse or counter punishes the *whole defense* flowing, and here only the
second level is flowing hard. Series football means picking the member of the series that beats the
specific reaction you saw. On second-and-4 an inside run that only needs four yards is also exactly
the right risk.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3.** First-and-10. The offense is under center with two tight ends, and Z is lined up unusually
tight on the right, about eight yards from the ball and a yard off the line, *inside* the cornerback. The
running back stands seven yards deep, slightly offset away from Z. The Sam linebacker is lined up outside
the tight end, between the tight end and Z. If this is the run it looks like, what is it, which defender
will Z block, who blocks the cornerback, and what should the cornerback do about it?

```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: a condensed two-tight-end set. Z (green ring) is about 8½ yards from the ball, a yard off the line and inside the cornerback (CB, ringed), who is lined up a yard and a half outside him. The Sam linebacker (S) is between the tight end and Z. The running back (R) is about seven yards deep."
off = check_legal(line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.8, -0.6, "R"),
                            O("Y", "TE", LINE_D, 4.8), O("U", "TE", LINE_D, -4.8),
                            O("Z", "WR", OFF_D, 8.6), O("X", "WR", OFF_D, -9.5)])
dfn = front(pe=("9", 5.7), pt=("3", 2.35), bt=("1", -0.7), be=("5", -4.0),
            lbs=(("WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.5, 1.4, "M"), ("SAM", 4.2, 7.0, "S")),
            cb=(-11.0, 10.2), safeties=((12.0, -6.5), (11.0, 7.5)))
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 3: condensed split, back deep")
p.highlight("Z", color=style.THIRD); p.highlight("RCB", color=style.DEFENSE)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-14.0, 15.0), window=(-8.5, 14.5))
say(fld, p, -3.4, 10.6, "Z: inside\nthe corner", color=GREEN, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A crack-toss to the right, as in @fig-crack-seal.** The tells: a receiver lined up *inside* the
cornerback (a wide receiver has no reason to start there on a run unless he is going to block back
inside), a tight end on the same side to seal the end, and a back deep enough to take a pitch and get
outside. **Z cracks the Sam**, the force player he is already lined up beside. **A pulling lineman,
often the right tackle, replaces him on the cornerback.**

**The cornerback's answer:** watch Z, not the backfield. The moment Z turns inside, he yells "crack!" and
comes up hard to become the force player himself, *outside* the ball, ideally before the pulling tackle
reaches him. That turns the back inside, toward the pursuit. If the corner gets caught watching the
backfield, he gets blocked by a 310-pound tackle in space. The offense's counter to a corner who
crack-replaces aggressively is to fake the crack and throw over him: Z steps inside, the corner jumps up,
and Z turns upfield on a route. One alignment, two plays, and the corner has to be right about which.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- Outside runs are a **race** between the ball and the defense's pursuit. The defense wins it with a
  **force** player who turns the ball back inside and everyone else pursuing fast. Perimeter plays punish
  a slow defense; misdirection punishes a fast one, and each family needs the other.
- Two blocks make outside runs work: the **crack block**, a receiver or wing hitting an inside defender
  from the side (above the waist, by rule), and the **seal block**, walling a defender off rather than
  moving him. Together with a puller replacing the cracking receiver, they make the **crack-toss**.
- The **jet sweep** turns jet motion's running start into a race the defense starts a step behind, and
  pulls the linebackers sideways even when the ball goes elsewhere. **End-arounds** (one exchange) and
  **reverses** (two) send the ball back against the flow and live or die on the backside end.
- The **Wing-T** organized all of this as **series football**: the **buck sweep** and the plays that
  look identical for one second and punish each reaction to it (the trap, the **waggle**, the counter).
  Its children are the NFL's jet sweeps, buck sweeps from the shotgun and bootlegs.
- **Eye candy** is motion or a fake that holds defenders without blocking them. Half a second is about
  three yards, which is a gap. It works only as long as the motion is sometimes real.
- Receiver runs are rare (under one per team-game) and, on average, much more valuable than running back
  carries, with more lost-yardage plays. They are **constraint plays**: their value comes from the base
  plays they punish, which is why you can't simply run them more.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**From diagrams to real tracking data.** The two animations in this chapter are gridiron simulations in
Big Data Bowl (BDB) coordinates, so real tracking data drops into the same drawing code. The 2025 Big
Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) flags, for every player on every play, whether he was in
motion at the snap, and records who carried the ball, so you can pull every run by a wide receiver who
was moving at the snap (most of them jet sweeps) and watch the linebackers' first steps for yourself.
The data is hosted on Kaggle and needs a free login, so this code is not run when the book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
player_play = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/player_play.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")

# ball carriers on designed runs, with their roster position
carriers = player_play[player_play["hadRushAttempt"] == 1].merge(players[["nflId", "position"]], on="nflId")
jets = carriers[(carriers["position"] == "WR") & (carriers["inMotionAtBallSnap"] == True)]  # noqa: E712
print(len(jets), "runs by a wide receiver in motion at the snap")

g, pl = jets.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[-1.0, 0.0, 0.6, 1.4])   # same call as the simulated plays
```
:::

[^backblock]: An offensive player may not block an opponent from behind, in the back, above the waist
    (illegal block above the waist, a 10-yard foul; contact from behind below the waist is clipping):
    NFL rulebook, Rule 12, Section 1, linked from <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>;
    summary at <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_in_the_back>. "Aim at the near number" is the
    common coaching cue for a legal crack.

[^backside]: On why defenses now keep the backside end home against bootlegs rather than letting him
    crash down the line, and how he "slow plays" the fake and then breaks on the boot: Dusty Evely, "When
    Open Isn't Open Part 2: PA Boot," March 4, 2023, <https://dustyevely.substack.com/p/when-open-isnt-open-part-2-pa-boot>.
    "Boot, counter, reverse" is the usual coaching checklist for this player; the run-fit details are in
    [05-05](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).

[^crackrule]: *2026 Official Playing Rules of the National Football League*, Rule 12, Section 2,
    Article 6, "Crackback Block": the block occurs within five yards on either side of the line of
    scrimmage by a player moving toward the spot of the snap who was set more than two yards outside a
    tackle, or was in the backfield and moved that wide or was in motion at the snap; prohibited contact
    is below the waist or any contact banned against a defenseless player (Article 9(b)(1–3)); loss of
    15 yards. Rulebook PDF linked from <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.

[^blindside]: NFL, "Health and safety-related rules changes since 2002." A 2009 rule had already
    banned blindside blocks to the head or neck; the 2019 change made it a foul if a player "initiates a
    block when his path is toward or parallel to his own end line and makes forcible contact to his
    opponent with his helmet, forearm, or shoulder." The current text (Rule 12-2-7) exempts contact in the
    close-line area before the ball has left it:
    <https://www.nfl.com/playerhealthandsafety/equipment-and-innovation/rules-changes/nfl-health-and-safety-related-rules-changes-since-2002>.

[^threestrike]: The 2026 NFL/NFLPA three-strike policy (hip-drop tackles, horse-collar tackles, launching,
    hits on a defenseless player and blindside blocks; three in a season means a one-game suspension):
    <https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/nfls-new-three-strike-system-doesnt-apply-until-the-2026-regular-season>.
    Agreed by the league and the players' union in August 2026; it begins with the 2026 regular season,
    and preseason fouls do not count.

[^popPass]: A pass is forward if the ball is thrown toward the opponent's goal line, however short the
    distance (NFL Rule 8, Section 1); a flip that travels forward to a receiver crossing in front of the
    quarterback is therefore a forward pass and is scored as a completion, not a run, and a forward pass
    that hits the ground before anyone catches it is incomplete (Rule 8), so a dropped flip is not a fumble. Example: Tyreek
    Hill's 1-yard touchdown on a jet-motion shovel at the Chargers on Sept. 9, 2018 is recorded in the
    play-by-play as "P.Mahomes pass short middle to T.Hill," with the throw 3 yards behind the line
    (nflverse; course check).

[^raymond]: University of Delaware, "Blue Hens Rewind: Tubby Raymond wins 300th career game" (Raymond's
    300th win came on Nov. 10, 2001, 10–6 over Richmond; he retired at 300–119–3):
    <https://bluehens.com/news/2020/10/17/football-blue-hens-rewind-tubby-raymond-wins-300th-career-game-in-defensive-battle.aspx>;
    Nelson's years (1951–1965) and the Wing-T's origins: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware_Fightin%27_Blue_Hens_football>;
    College Football Hall of Fame: <https://cfbhall.com/inductees/tubby-raymond-2003>. Raymond's Michigan
    degree (1950), his years as Nelson's assistant, and his acrylic portraits of Delaware seniors:

    developing the Wing-T at Maine (1949–50): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_M._Nelson>.

[^orderbook]: Harold R. "Tubby" Raymond and Ted Kempski, *The Delaware Wing-T: An Order of Football*

[^brown]: Chris B. Brown, "The Making of a Modern-Day Guru," Grantland, January 3, 2014:
